title: One Fare, End to End: A Slow Rider's Guide to the 501 Queen

blocks.text: The 501 is the cheapest long, slow look at Toronto you can buy. For a single fare you can sit by a window and watch the city change block by block - from the Humber bridges in the west to the last loop near the lake in the east, through Victorian main streets, glass towers, parkland and a beach. It takes roughly ninety minutes if you never get off. This is a guide to doing exactly that, and to the handful of places worth breaking the ride for.

I wrote it because the 501 is easy to ride and hard to *see*. Most of us know it as the streetcar that is late, or the one that gets short-turned two stops early, or the line of replacement buses on a summer construction weekend. Riding it end to end on purpose, with nothing waiting at the far end, turns it into something else: a window-seat survey of how the city is patched together.

blocks.title: Check the TTC before you go
blocks.text: The 501 is routinely split into sections, short-turned, or replaced by buses for track work, events and construction. 'End to end' often means a change of vehicle at a division point. Nothing below is a timetable - check the TTC trip planner on the morning you ride, and treat the routes here as a way to read the street, not a schedule.

The useful mental model is that Queen is less a single ride than a corridor with a number painted on it. It is one of the oldest continuous streetcar lines in the city, and it behaves like old infrastructure: dependable in spirit, improvised in practice. Know these six things and the whole trip becomes easy.

items: **It is often run in pieces.** On many days the line is split at a downtown division point and you change vehicles to carry on. Ask the operator whether the car goes all the way rather than assuming it does.
**One fare covers the lot.** Tap a PRESTO card or a contactless payment as you board. The transfer is time-based, so you can get off, wander and re-board within the window without paying twice.
**Board through any door** on the newer cars and keep your proof of payment with you - fare inspectors do get on.
**Streetcars share the street.** They stop in the right lane, not at a platform, so you wait on the sidewalk and step out into traffic. Watch for cyclists and drivers passing on the right.
**Service is frequent but not clockwork.** The line runs from early morning until after midnight. Allow slack; do not build a tight connection around it.
**Westbound heads for the Humber, eastbound for Neville Park and the Beaches.** Get this backwards and you simply see the city in reverse, which is also a perfectly good afternoon.

blocks.text: What you notice from a window seat

From a car window the city stops being a list of neighbourhoods and becomes a continuous thing. Brick gives way to glass and then to brick again. A street that is all cheap storefronts turns, one intersection later, into a street of careful renovations. The 501 does not skip the in-between parts the way the subway does, and the in-between parts are most of Toronto.
A subway shows you where the city decided to put people. A streetcar shows you what was already there.
Do not think of it as one long trip. Think of it as three short ones with the same seat. Here is how the street tends to unfold, west to east.

blocks.title: Act I - The west, from the Humber to Parkdale
stops: Start at the **Humber loop** where the line begins near the river and the old bridge. The city feels almost like a small town here.
Roll through **Roncesvalles** - Polish bakeries, low shopfronts, wide sidewalks - and watch the dense residential streets begin.
At **Parkdale**, the storefronts get scruffier and more interesting. This is the stretch worth getting off for coffee if the car is crowded.
By **Dufferin**, the downtown skyline starts to appear in gaps between the buildings.
blocks.note: This is the quietest act. Go in the morning, take a seat on the right eastbound, and let the city arrive gradually.

blocks.title: Act II - Downtown, from Queen West to Yonge
stops: **Trinity Bellwoods to Spadina**: the busiest retail stretch on the line, all design shops, cafés and foot traffic.
**City Hall and Osgoode**: the street suddenly becomes civic and formal - big stone, big setbacks, the towers of the financial district behind them.
**Queen and Yonge**: the nominal centre of the grid, and usually the most crowded stop. Expect a shuffle of people and a pause.
East of Yonge the towers thin out and the older, lower city reappears almost immediately.
blocks.note: If you only have half an hour, ride this act. It contains the whole argument about how Toronto changed in one generation.

blocks.title: Act III - The east, from Moss Park to the lake
stops: **Moss Park to Parliament**: a plainer, quieter Queen, with wide intersections and long blocks.
**Riverdale and Leslieville**: the retail comes back, smaller and more independent, and the houses get taller and narrower.
**The Beaches**: the street slows down, the shops turn seasonal, and you can suddenly see the lake at the bottom of the side streets.
Finish at **Neville Park**, where the car turns around and everyone gets out. Walk two minutes south and you are at the water.
blocks.note: Save this act for late afternoon. Ending at the lake on a clear day is the whole point of riding east in the first place.

blocks.text: Three stops worth getting off for

You can ride the whole thing without moving, but these are the places where a twenty-minute detour repays the fare. Details are deliberately loose - these are neighbourhoods, not booked attractions, so check hours before you go.

blocks.name: Trinity Bellwoods Park
blocks.area: Queen St W at Ossington Ave
blocks.vibe: The best free interruption on the line. A big sloped lawn, old trees, a dog bowl that is basically a small lake, and a steady parade of the neighbourhood. Queen West's shops and bakeries are a block away, so the move is simple: get off, buy something, come back and sit.
blocks.address: Queen St W near Ossington Ave, Toronto
blocks.transit: 501 Queen at Ossington; also handy for the Ossington and College buses
blocks.parking: Street parking is tight - the streetcar is the point
blocks.bestFor: A picnic, dogs, a chapter of a book, watching the city go past
blocks.tip: The park slopes down from Queen. Walk to the bottom and turn around for the best view back up at the houses.

blocks.name: The Queen West strip
blocks.area: Queen St W, Spadina to Bathurst
blocks.vibe: A few blocks of the densest, most self-conscious retail in the city - bookshops, record stores, small clothing labels and a lot of very good coffee. It changes faster than any other stretch on the line, so half the fun is seeing what replaced what since your last ride.
blocks.address: Queen St W between Spadina Ave and Bathurst St, Toronto
blocks.transit: 501 Queen; a short walk from the Spadina or Bathurst buses
blocks.parking: Green P lots nearby, but walking from the stop is easier
blocks.bestFor: A rainy afternoon, browsing without a list, a proper coffee
blocks.tip: Walk it east to west rather than riding through it. The shopfronts are meant to be seen at three kilometres an hour, not thirty.

blocks.name: Kew Gardens & the Beaches
blocks.area: Queen St E near Lee Ave
blocks.vibe: Where the streetcar finally runs out of city. A lakeside park, a boardwalk, a beach and a main street that still feels like a main street. Get off at the east end, walk south to the water, and the ninety-minute ride suddenly makes sense.
blocks.address: Queen St E at Lee Ave, Toronto (a short walk to the lake)
blocks.transit: 501 Queen eastbound to the Neville Park area
blocks.parking: Street parking on the side streets; busy on summer weekends
blocks.bestFor: Ending the trip, a swim in season, ice cream, doing nothing
blocks.tip: Go on a weekday if you can. On a hot Saturday the whole line seems to be heading for the same patch of sand.

blocks.text: The unwritten rules of a long ride
Nobody hands you a rulebook at the stop. These are the small courtesies that make a two-hour sit pleasant for everyone in the car.

items: **Move in, then sit.** On a crowded car, walk toward the middle before claiming a seat so people boarding behind you are not stuck at the door.
**Give up the priority seats** near the front without being asked, and keep the aisle clear of bags and feet.
**Take off a backpack** when the car is full. It takes two seconds and buys a surprising amount of goodwill.
**Keep the volume down** - headphones, not speakers, and phone calls kept short and quiet.
**Let people off before you push on**, and use the rear doors to board when the front is jammed.
**Have your fare ready** before the doors open so the whole car is not waiting while you find a card.
**Do not block the window** for a photo at the exact moment the light changes. There is always another stop.

blocks.title: The cheapest city tour in Toronto
blocks.text: For one fare you get a couple of hours of the best people-watching in town. Go mid-morning on a weekday, take a window seat, and deliberately leave the return trip unplanned. The whole point is that nothing is waiting at the other end.

items: A PRESTO card or a contactless card with a tapped fare ready to go
Headphones - but one ear free enough to hear stop announcements
A book or a notebook for the stretches between the interesting bits
A layer of some kind; the older cars run warm, the newer ones cool
A phone with the TTC trip planner open for the service alerts
Water and something small to eat if you plan to get off and walk
No fixed schedule at the far end - this is the most important item

blocks.text: Almost any time works, but the ride changes character with the clock. A few rules of thumb, none of them strict:

items: **Weekday mid-morning** is the sweet spot: light crowds, good window light, and a car that mostly moves.
**Late afternoon eastbound** puts the low sun behind you and ends at the lake at the best hour.
**Rush hour** is the worst time for a slow ride and the best time to remember you are not in a hurry. Avoid it on your first attempt.
**Summer weekends** mean construction diversions and packed cars near the Beaches - check the alerts before committing.
**A grey, drizzly day** is secretly ideal. The windows fog, the colours flatten, and the whole city looks like a photograph.

blocks.text: That is the line. Start wherever you are closest, ride one act or all three, and get off at least once for no particular reason. If you find a stop worth writing about - or a diversion that has changed since this went up - tell me and I will fold it into the next issue. Now go find a window seat.
